extracted.intended_audience: orators, prose writers, and students of rhetoric/classical style
extracted.subtask_short: writing sublimity in prose and oratory
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing 'the sublime' in prose and oratory, covering structure, amplification, imitation, imagery, and rhetorical figures. Emphasizes when and how devices like apostrophe, imagination, and amplification produce grandeur without artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected, undignified, or pedantic intervening
rubrics_metrics.description: “allowing nothing affected or undignified or pedantic to intervene.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrelevancies spoil the effect of sublime ideas; they are like gaps or open tracery in architecture and 'utterly spoil' a coherent structure. Make a clean sweep of main points by order of merit and bring them together, excluding affected or pedantic touches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimitation and arrangement of main points into a single whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The delimitation of the main points and their arrangement so as to form a single whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect the principal points in order of merit and arrange them coherently so nothing irrelevant interrupts the structure; this ordering and unity strengthen the sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification consists in accumulating all the aspects and topics inherent in the subject and thus strengthening the argument by dwelling upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many methods (development of a commonplace, exaggeration, laying stress on events or arguments, careful husbandry of facts or feelings). Amplification always goes with quantity and a degree of redundancy; it strengthens by accumulation but cannot alone create sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Sublimity vs Amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sublimity lies in elevation, amplification rather in amount; and so you often find sublimity in a single idea, whereas amplification always goes with quantity and a certain degree of redundance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity can arise from a single elevated idea; amplification is about breadth and reiteration. Do not conflate the two: techniques of amplification amplify but require sublimity (elevation) to form a perfect whole; amplification differs from proof (which demonstrates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paths to sublimity: natural genius, imitation, imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity in ideas is produced by natural genius or imitation or imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these as distinct sources: innate genius, zealous imitation/emulation of great writers, or imaginative depiction. Each can produce sublimity when properly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zealous imitation/emulation of great authors
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Zealous imitation of the great historians and poets of the past.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and emulate Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Thucydides, etc.; imagine how they would have said or reacted to your passage. Borrowing is not theft but taking an impression from fine characters; emulate to reach ideal standards of perfection and to irrigate your own style from their sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images / imagination to produce weight, grandeur, and energy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Weight, grandeur, and energy in writing are very largely produced ... by the use of “images.”’ Imagination brings vivid mental pictures so you and your audience 'see' what is described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In oratory imagination should present ideas clearly and, when combined with argumentative treatment, can convince and even master the audience. Distinguish imaginative aims of poetry (enthral) and prose (clarify), and aim for realism in rhetoric except where poetic extravagance is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative passages in oratory: favor reality and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The most perfect effect of imagination in oratory is always one of reality and truth; poetic/romantic exaggeration that exceeds credibility is inappropriate for rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid outlandish, clearly impossible scenes in forensic oratory (e.g., literal sightings of Furies) because they stray into theatricality; rhetorical imagination should stay persuasive and believable, though vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of apostrophe/adjuration (single powerful figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the single figure of adjuration (apostrophe) to transform argument into transcendent sublimity—e.g., Demosthenes’ oath: 'It cannot be that you were wrong; no, by those who bore the brunt at Marathon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An oath or apostrophe is not inherently sublime: consider place, manner, circumstances, and motive. Design such figures to suit audience feelings and purpose (e.g., to console the defeated, to eulogize ancestors); avoid using an oath out of context where it merely wanders or does not immortalize its referent (contrast Eupolis vs Demosthenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between intensity (sublimity) and diffuseness (diffusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demosthenes’ strength is in rugged sublimity, Cicero’s in diffusion. Intensity (violent emotion, speed, force) 'dumbfounds' the audience; diffuseness overwhelms by a rolling conflagration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intensity when you need sudden, overwhelming force; use diffuseness for perorations, digressions, descriptive/show passages, history, natural philosophy, or when you wish to overwhelm rather than stun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures (rhetorical devices) are allies of the sublime but must be concealed
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures seem to be natural allies of the sublime and draw reinforcement from the alliance; yet they give a suggestion of treachery when unconscionably used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures are most effective when they conceal the fact of being figures—brilliance conceals artifice. An obvious figure suggests craft or fallacy and may provoke hostility from authoritative listeners; craft should be hidden in a halo of grandeur. Use figures to enhance, not to substitute, for genuine sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conspicuous artifices before judges, rulers, or despots
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an inevitable suspicion attaching to the unconscionable use of figures... especially when your speech is addressed to a judge with absolute authority, or still more to a despot, a king, or a ruler in high place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing authority, avoid treating the audience like children or attempting to outwit them with ostentatious devices; such tactics may provoke hostility. Temper rhetorical artifice with dignity and concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure every word; temper passion with restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In the very whirlwind of passion you must beget a temperance.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in passionate passages, choose words carefully to preempt objections and preserve credibility (example: Demosthenes avoids naming a successful result where it would invite rebuttal). Balance emotional force with measured language to maintain persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification techniques (examples and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification may be done by the development of a commonplace, or by exaggeration, or by laying stress on events or arguments, or by careful husbandry of facts or feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are 'ten thousand kinds' of amplification; use varied techniques (accumulation, piling-on effect) but recognize their limits—without sublimity these methods can produce a nerveless or hollow result. Exception: in passages aiming at pity or depreciation the effect required may differ.
